title: Ὀλοοίτροχος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The two Ajaxes and their men speak to one another, glad with a joy that a god has put in them, while the earth-shaker rouses the rest of the Achaeans, who are resting behind by the ships and grieving to see the Trojans inside the wall. He goes to the captains and, in a long speech, shames them: the Trojans, once like frightened deer, now fight at the ships, and whatever Agamemnon's fault, the army may not slacken, for Hector has broken the gates. The Achaeans close their ranks round the two Ajaxes, shield on shield. Hector leads the Trojans down on them like a boulder hurled from a cliff by a winter torrent, which runs on until it reaches level ground. He is stopped by the close lines, driven back, and shouts to his men that Zeus is with him. Deiphobus advances behind his shield, and Meriones' spear breaks on it; Meriones goes to his hut for another.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον
χάρμῃ γηθόσυνοι, τήν σφιν θεὸς ἔμβαλε θυμῷ·
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon
charmēi gēthosynoi, tēn sphin theos embale thymōi·
sentences.l:
So they, on the one hand, such things to one another were speaking,
glad with the joy of battle, which for them a god cast into their heart;
sentences.i: So they spoke such words to one another, glad with the joy of battle that a god had cast into their hearts;
sentences.n: This takes up the previous part: the two Ajaxes, each stirred by Poseidon, have been speaking to one another, and ὣς οἳ μέν ‘so they, on the one hand’ sums up those speeches; the μέν is answered by τόφρα δέ ‘but meanwhile’ in the next unit. A new paragraph begins here. τοιαῦτα is ‘such things’ (neuter plural of τοιοῦτος) and ἀγόρευον is the imperfect, ‘were speaking’. χάρμῃ is the dative of χάρμη ‘joy of battle’, the word the table uses throughout, and γηθόσυνοι ‘glad’ agrees with οἳ; τήν is the relative and points back to χάρμῃ, with σφιν ‘for them’ (epic for σφίσιν) and θυμῷ ‘in the heart’ (singular, one heart for the group). The god who put it there is not named; the next unit shows him at work. Line 81 is the same as 5.274, and the English of that line is kept.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δὲ τοὺς ὄπιθεν γαιήοχος ὦρσεν Ἀχαιούς,
οἳ παρὰ νηυσὶ θοῇσιν ἀνέψυχον φίλον ἦτορ.
sentences.tr:
tophra de tous opithen gaiēochos ōrsen Achaious,
hoi para nēusi thoēisin anepsychon philon ētor.
sentences.l:
But meanwhile those behind, the earth-holder roused, the Achaeans,
who beside the swift ships were cooling again their dear heart.
sentences.i: But meanwhile the earth-holder roused the Achaeans who were in the rear, the men who were refreshing their hearts beside the swift ships.
sentences.n: Poseidon, still unnamed, now turns from the Ajaxes to the rest of the army. τόφρα δέ ‘but meanwhile’ answers the μέν of the line before. τοὺς ὄπιθεν … Ἀχαιούς is ‘the Achaeans behind’, those held back in the rear: the article τούς is the pointing kind, and the adverb ὄπιθεν sits between it and the noun. γαιήοχος ‘earth-holder’ is a stock title of Poseidon, as ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’ will be at 89, and both are translated every time; the poet does not name him in this part. ὦρσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. ἀνέψυχον is the imperfect of ἀναψύχω ‘cool again’, said of the heart, so ‘were refreshing’; φίλον ἦτορ is the stock phrase ‘dear heart’; θοῇσιν is the epic dative plural feminine of θοός ‘swift’ (Attic θοαῖς).

sentences.t: τῶν ῥ’ ἅμα τ’ ἀργαλέῳ καμάτῳ φίλα γυῖα λέλυντο,
sentences.tr: tōn rh’ hama t’ argaleōi kamatōi phila guia lelynto,
sentences.l: Of them, along with grievous weariness, the dear limbs were loosened,
sentences.i: Their limbs were slack with grievous weariness,
sentences.n: Why they are resting: they are worn out. τῶν ‘of them’ (the rear Achaeans) is a genitive of possession with γυῖα ‘limbs’; ῥ’ is ῥα, a particle meaning ‘so, as one would expect’. ἅμα takes the dative here, ‘along with’, so the limbs and the weariness go together: ἀργαλέῳ καμάτῳ is ‘with grievous weariness’ (κάματος ‘weariness’, ἀργαλέος ‘grievous’). λέλυντο is the pluperfect passive of λύω ‘loosen’, ‘had been loosened’, i.e. were slack; φίλα ‘dear’ is the ordinary Homeric word for what is one’s own. The unit ends at the comma, and the sentence continues.

sentences.t:
καί σφιν ἄχος κατὰ θυμὸν ἐγίγνετο δερκομένοισι
Τρῶας, τοὶ μέγα τεῖχος ὑπερκατέβησαν ὁμίλῳ.
sentences.tr:
kai sphin achos kata thymon egigneto derkomenoisi
Trōas, toi mega teichos hyperkatebēsan homilōi.
sentences.l:
and for them grief in their heart arose as they looked
at the Trojans, who the great wall came down over in a throng.
sentences.i: and grief arose in their hearts as they looked at the Trojans, who had come down over the great wall in a throng.
sentences.n: The cause of their grief is the sight of the Trojans inside the wall. σφιν ‘for them’ goes with the participle δερκομένοισι ‘looking’ (dative plural of δέρκομαι), so ‘grief arose for them, as they looked’; ἄχος ‘grief’ is the subject of ἐγίγνετο, an imperfect, ‘was arising’, and κατὰ θυμόν ‘in the heart’. τοί is the epic form of the relative οἵ. ὑπερκατέβησαν is ὑπέρ + κατά + ἔβησαν ‘went down over’, with τεῖχος ‘wall’ the accusative of what was crossed (compare ὑπέρβασαν at 12.469, which is this crossing); ὁμίλῳ ‘in a throng’ is a dative of manner.

sentences.t: τοὺς οἵ γ’ εἰσορόωντες ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι δάκρυα λεῖβον·
sentences.tr: tous hoi g’ eisoroōntes hyp’ ophrysi dakrya leibon·
sentences.l: Them, they, looking at, from beneath their brows tears were pouring;
sentences.i: Looking at them, they let tears fall from beneath their brows;
sentences.n: Their tears. τοὺς … εἰσορόωντες is ‘looking at them’, where τούς is the Trojans of the line before and εἰσορόωντες the uncontracted epic participle of εἰσοράω (Attic εἰσορῶντες); οἵ γε is ‘they’, the Achaeans, with γε making the pronoun emphatic. λεῖβον is the imperfect of λείβω ‘pour, let fall’. ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι ‘beneath the brows’ is the picture of tears running out from under the eyebrows, as in the Odyssey’s phrase for a tear shed beneath the brows.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἔφαν φεύξεσθαι ὑπ’ ἐκ κακοῦ·
sentences.tr: ou gar ephan pheuxesthai hyp’ ek kakou·
sentences.l: for they did not say that they would flee out from under the evil;
sentences.i: for they did not think they would escape from this evil;
sentences.n: The reason for the tears: they thought they were lost. ἔφαν is the imperfect of φημί ‘say’, and here ‘they said (to themselves), they thought’, with the future infinitive φεύξεσθαι ‘would flee, would escape’. ὑπ’ ἐκ, the same as ὑπέκ, is ‘out from under’, two prepositions that stand side by side; they go with κακοῦ ‘evil’, the evil seen as a weight over them. The unit stops at the ano teleia in the middle of the line, and ἀλλά opens the contrast.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐνοσίχθων
ῥεῖα μετεισάμενος κρατερὰς ὄτρυνε φάλαγγας.
sentences.tr:
all’ enosichthōn
rheia meteisamenos krateras otryne phalangas.
sentences.l:
but the earth-shaker,
easily going among them, urged on the strong battle-lines.
sentences.i: but the earth-shaker, going easily among them, urged on the strong battle-lines.
sentences.n: Poseidon, still unnamed, is the earth-shaker, ἐνοσίχθων (see γαιήοχος at 83). ῥεῖα is the epic ῥέα ‘easily’ (Attic ῥᾳδίως). μετεισάμενος is an aorist middle participle, ‘going among (them)’, with no object stated; its sense comes from the verb it governs. κρατεράς is the Ionic form of καρτεράς, ‘strong’, the table’s word. ὄτρυνε is the aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’ (compare ὄρνυμι at 83). φάλαγγας ‘battle-lines’ is the object of ὄτρυνε.

sentences.t:
Τεῦκρον ἔπι πρῶτον καὶ Λήϊτον ἦλθε κελεύων
Πηνέλεών θ’ ἥρωα Θόαντά τε Δηΐπυρόν τε
Μηριόνην τε καὶ Ἀντίλοχον μήστωρας ἀϋτῆς·
sentences.tr:
Teukron epi prōton kai Lēïton ēlthe keleuōn
Pēneleōn th’ hērōa Thoanta te Dēïpyron te
Mērionēn te kai Antilochon mēstōras aÿtēs·
sentences.i: First he went to Teucer and Leitus, bidding them on, and to the hero Peneleos and Thoas and Deipyrus, and to Meriones and Antilochus, masters of the battle-cry;
sentences.n: The captains he rouses are listed. Τεῦκρον ἔπι is ‘to Teucer’: the preposition ἐπί stands after its noun (hence the accent on ἔπι), and the other names, joined by τε and καί, hang on it. ἦλθε κελεύων is ‘went, bidding’ (κελεύω ‘bid, order’). ἥρωα is the plain title ‘hero’, in the accusative with Πηνέλεων (Peneleos, with the θ’ for τε elided after it). Δηΐπυρον has the diaeresis as printed. μήστωρας ἀϋτῆς is the house rendering ‘masters of the battle-cry’ (μήστωρ ‘counsellor, planner’, ἀϋτή ‘battle-cry’), in apposition to Meriones and Antilochus.

sentences.t: τοὺς ὅ γ’ ἐποτρύνων ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: tous ho g’ epotrynōn epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: Them he, urging on, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Urging them on, he spoke winged words to them:
sentences.n: The speech introduction: the speaker is Poseidon. τούς ‘them’ means the captains, and ὅ γε ‘he’ is Poseidon, the pronoun made emphatic by γε. ἐποτρύνων is the participle of ἐποτρύνω ‘urge on’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘he spoke winged words’ is the stock formula, with προσηύδα the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. One accusative, τούς, serves both the participle and the verb of speaking, ‘urging them on, he spoke … to them’.

sentences.t: αἰδὼς Ἀργεῖοι, κοῦροι νέοι·
sentences.tr: aidōs Argeioi, kouroi neoi·
sentences.l: “Shame, Argives, youths, young ones;
sentences.i: “Shame, Argives, you young men!
sentences.n: Poseidon’s speech opens on a cry rather than a sentence. αἰδώς ‘shame’ is the nominative of αἰδώς used as an exclamation, as at 5.787 (αἰδὼς Ἀργεῖοι). Ἀργεῖοι ‘Argives’ and κοῦροι νέοι ‘young men, young ones’ are vocatives; the Iliad keeps the army’s three names apart, and here the speaker says ‘Argives’. κοῦρος is ‘young man’, and νέοι ‘young’ repeats it. The unit ends at the ano teleia, and the sentence of trust follows.

sentences.t:
ὔμμιν ἔγωγε
μαρναμένοισι πέποιθα σαωσέμεναι νέας ἁμάς·
sentences.tr:
ymmin egōge
marnamenoisi pepoitha saōsemenai neas hamas·
sentences.l:
In you, for my part, as you fight, I trust
to save our ships;
sentences.i: For my part, I trust you, as you fight, to save our ships;
sentences.n: The trust he places in them, before the rebuke. ὔμμιν is the epic form of ὑμῖν ‘you’ (dative), and ἔγωγε ‘I for my part’. πέποιθα is the perfect of πείθομαι with the sense of the present, ‘I trust’, here with the dative of the person, ὔμμιν, and the infinitive. μαρναμένοισι ‘as you fight’ is a dative plural participle agreeing with ὔμμιν. σαωσέμεναι is the epic future infinitive of σαόω ‘save’ (Attic σώσειν), so ‘trust you to save’ means ‘am confident that you will save’. ἁμάς is a Homeric form of ἡμετέρας ‘our’, agreeing with νέας (accusative plural).

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ὑμεῖς πολέμοιο μεθήσετε λευγαλέοιο,
νῦν δὴ εἴδεται ἦμαρ ὑπὸ Τρώεσσι δαμῆναι.
sentences.tr:
ei d’ hymeis polemoio methēsete leugaleoio,
nyn dē eidetai ēmar hypo Trōessi damēnai.
sentences.l:
but if you will slacken from pitiful war,
now indeed appears the day to be subdued by the Trojans.
sentences.i: but if you slacken in the pitiful war, then the day has surely come into view when we shall be overcome by the Trojans.
sentences.n: The warning. εἰ δέ ‘but if’ with the future indicative μεθήσετε ‘you will slacken’ states the case as a plain prospect; μεθίημι takes the genitive of what is let go, πολέμοιο (as at 4.234). λευγαλέοιο is ‘pitiful’, the table’s word for λευγαλέος, and agrees with πολέμοιο. εἴδεται is the middle of the verb for ‘seem, appear’ (as in κὴρ εἴδεται at 1.228), with ἦμαρ ‘day’ as its subject; ὑπὸ Τρώεσσι δαμῆναι (aorist passive infinitive of δάμνημι ‘subdue’) says what the day is, ‘a day to be subdued under the Trojans’, and the English supplies ‘when we shall be’.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ μέγα θαῦμα τόδ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρῶμαι
δεινόν, ὃ οὔ ποτ’ ἔγωγε τελευτήσεσθαι ἔφασκον,
Τρῶας ἐφ’ ἡμετέρας ἰέναι νέας,
sentences.tr:
ō popoi ē mega thauma tod’ ophthalmoisin horōmai
deinon, ho ou pot’ egōge teleutēsesthai ephaskon,
Trōas eph’ hēmeteras ienai neas,
sentences.l:
Ah, truly a great wonder this with my eyes I behold,
a dread one, which I never, for my part, said would be fulfilled,
the Trojans to our ships to be coming,
sentences.i: Ah, this is truly a great and dreadful wonder that I behold with my own eyes, one that I, for my part, never said would come to pass: that the Trojans would come against our ships,
sentences.n: Poseidon’s astonishment, which runs on into a simile. ὢ πόποι is the table’s ‘Ah’, and ἦ strengthens it, ‘truly’. θαῦμα ‘wonder’ is the object of ὁρῶμαι (middle of ὁράω, ‘look at, behold’) with ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ‘with my eyes’, and τόδ’ ‘this’ and δεινόν ‘dread’ both agree with it. ὃ οὔ ποτε … ἔφασκον is a relative clause on θαῦμα: ἔφασκον is the iterative imperfect of φημί ‘I used to say’, and τελευτήσεσθαι the future middle infinitive of τελευτάω, ‘would be accomplished’. Τρῶας ἐφ’ ἡμετέρας ἰέναι νέας (ἰέναι the infinitive of εἶμι ‘go, come’) says what the wonder is, ‘the Trojans coming against our ships’, with ἐπί and the accusative of the goal. The unit ends at the comma and the relative clause that begins the simile follows.

sentences.t:
οἳ τὸ πάρος περ
φυζακινῇς ἐλάφοισιν ἐοίκεσαν,
sentences.tr:
hoi to paros per
phyzakinēis elaphoisin eoikesan,
sentences.l:
who formerly, indeed,
to flight-prone deer were like,
sentences.i: who before this were like timid deer,
sentences.n: The simile begins by saying what the Trojans used to be. οἳ ‘who’ has Τρῶας as its antecedent, and τὸ πάρος περ is ‘formerly, even before’. φυζακινῇς is a rare adjective built on φύζα ‘flight, panic’, ‘given to flight’, rendered ‘flight-prone’ in l and ‘timid’ in the English. ἐλάφοισιν is the epic dative plural of ἔλαφος ‘deer’ (the table’s word) and goes with ἐοίκεσαν, an epic past form of ἔοικα ‘be like’, which takes the dative.

sentences.t:
αἵ τε καθ’ ὕλην
θώων παρδαλίων τε λύκων τ’ ἤϊα πέλονται
αὔτως ἠλάσκουσαι ἀνάλκιδες, οὐδ’ ἔπι χάρμη·
sentences.tr:
hai te kath’ hylēn
thōōn pardaliōn te lykōn t’ ēïa pelontai
autōs ēlaskousai analkides, oud’ epi charmē·
sentences.i: which in the forest become food for jackals, leopards and wolves as they roam idly, without might, and with no joy of battle in them;
sentences.n: What the deer are: prey, with no strength and no spirit. αἵ τε ‘which’ refers to the deer, and the τε marks a general truth, as often in similes. θώων … ἤϊα πέλονται is ‘are the food of jackals…’: ἤϊα is a plural noun ‘provisions, food’ (the sense is secure though its derivation is not), θώων is the genitive of θώς, usually taken to be the jackal, παρδαλίων of πάρδαλις ‘leopard’, and λύκων of λύκος ‘wolf’. αὔτως is ‘idly, to no purpose’; ἠλάσκουσαι is the participle of ἠλάσκω ‘roam’ (the table’s word, 2.470), and ἀνάλκιδες is ‘without might’ (ἀν- with ἀλκή ‘might’, as in the table). οὐδ’ ἔπι χάρμη: ἔπι is ἔπεστι ‘is upon, is in them’, and χάρμη is ‘joy of battle’, as at 82.

sentences.t:
ὣς Τρῶες τὸ πρίν γε μένος καὶ χεῖρας Ἀχαιῶν
μίμνειν οὐκ ἐθέλεσκον ἐναντίον, οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν·
sentences.tr:
hōs Trōes to prin ge menos kai cheiras Achaiōn
mimnein ouk etheleskon enantion, oud’ ēbaion·
sentences.l:
So the Trojans, formerly at least, the might and the hands of the Achaeans
were not willing to await, face to face, not even a little;
sentences.i: So the Trojans, before now, were never willing to stand up to the might and the hands of the Achaeans face to face, not the least bit;
sentences.n: The simile is applied: the Trojans were once the deer. ὣς ‘so’ closes the comparison; τὸ πρίν γε is ‘formerly at least’. μένος καὶ χεῖρας Ἀχαιῶν ‘the might and the hands of the Achaeans’ are the objects of μίμνειν (infinitive of μίμνω = μένω ‘wait for, stand up to’); χεῖρας ‘hands’ stands for the fighting strength of those hands, and μένος is ‘might’, as at 2.387. ἐθέλεσκον is the iterative imperfect of ἐθέλω, ‘they would (each time) be unwilling’. ἐναντίον is ‘face to face’, and οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν ‘not even a little’ (ἠβαιός ‘little, slight’, used as an adverb).

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ ἑκὰς πόλιος κοίλῃς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ μάχονται
ἡγεμόνος κακότητι μεθημοσύνῃσί τε λαῶν,
sentences.tr:
nyn de hekas polios koilēis epi nēusi machontai
hēgemonos kakotēti methēmosynēisi te laōn,
sentences.l:
but now far from the city, by the hollow ships, they fight,
through the leader’s baseness and the slackness of the people,
sentences.i: but now they fight far from the city, at the hollow ships, through the baseness of their leader and the slackness of the people,
sentences.n: The change since then, and whom Poseidon blames for it. ἑκάς ‘far’ takes the genitive πόλιος (the epic form of πόλεως) ‘from the city’; κοίλῃς ἐπὶ νηυσί is ‘at the hollow ships’, with κοίλῃς the epic feminine dative plural. ἡγεμόνος κακότητι is a dative of cause, ‘through the leader’s baseness’; κακότης is ‘baseness’ (the table, 2.368), and the leader, Agamemnon, is not named until line 112. μεθημοσύνῃσι is the dative plural of μεθημοσύνη ‘slackness’, from the verb μεθίημι ‘slacken’ (97), and λαῶν is ‘of the people’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
οἳ κείνῳ ἐρίσαντες ἀμυνέμεν οὐκ ἐθέλουσι
νηῶν ὠκυπόρων, ἀλλὰ κτείνονται ἀν’ αὐτάς.
sentences.tr:
hoi keinōi erisantes amynemen ouk ethelousi
nēōn ōkyporōn, alla kteinontai an’ autas.
sentences.l:
who, having quarrelled with that man, are not willing to defend
the swift-faring ships, but are being killed among them.
sentences.i: who, having quarrelled with him, are unwilling to defend the swift-faring ships, but are being killed among them.
sentences.n: Who these men are and what they have done. οἳ is the relative for λαῶν ‘the people’ in the line before. κείνῳ is the epic ἐκείνῳ ‘that man’, the leader, and ἐρίσαντες is the aorist participle of ἐρίζω ‘quarrel’ (the table’s word, 2.214), which takes the dative. ἀμυνέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἀμύνω ‘defend’ and takes the genitive νηῶν ‘the ships’; ὠκυπόρων is ‘swift-faring’. κτείνονται is the passive ‘are being killed’, and ἀν’ αὐτάς is ‘among them’, the ships.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰ δὴ καὶ πάμπαν ἐτήτυμον αἴτιός ἐστιν
ἥρως Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
οὕνεκ’ ἀπητίμησε ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα,
sentences.tr:
all’ ei dē kai pampan etētymon aitios estin
hērōs Atreïdēs eury kreiōn Agamemnōn
hounek’ apētimēse podōkea Pēleïōna,
sentences.l:
But if indeed even altogether in truth to blame is
the hero, Atreus’-son, wide-ruling Agamemnon,
because he dishonoured the fleet-footed son of Peleus,
sentences.i: But even if the hero Agamemnon, son of Atreus, wide-ruling, is in truth altogether to blame, because he dishonoured the fleet-footed son of Peleus,
sentences.n: He allows that Agamemnon may be at fault, and then says it changes nothing. ἀλλ’ εἰ δὴ καί is ‘but if indeed even’, and αἴτιος ‘to blame’ is a predicate adjective with ἐστιν; πάμπαν is ‘altogether’ and ἐτήτυμον ‘in truth’ (a neuter used as an adverb, the table’s word). Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ and εὐρὺ κρείων ‘wide-ruling’ (εὐρύ the adverb ‘widely’, κρείων ‘ruling’; the edition prints the two words apart) are the stock epithets of Agamemnon, translated every time; ἥρως is the plain title ‘hero’. ἀπητίμησε is ‘dishonoured’, the verb of the family of ἠτίμασεν at 1.11. ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα is ‘the fleet-footed son of Peleus’, Achilles, unnamed: ποδώκης is the table’s ‘fleet-footed’ and Πηλεΐων the patronymic ‘son of Peleus’. The unit ends at the comma, and the main clause follows.

sentences.t: ἡμέας γ’ οὔ πως ἔστι μεθιέμεναι πολέμοιο.
sentences.tr: hēmeas g’ ou pōs esti methiemenai polemoio.
sentences.l: us at least it is not in any way possible to slacken from war.
sentences.i: still, there is no way for us, at least, to slacken in the fighting.
sentences.n: The main clause: whatever the fault, the Achaeans may not slacken. ἡμέας is the epic form of ἡμᾶς ‘us’, the accusative subject of the infinitive, and γε limits it, ‘us at least’. οὔ πως ἔστι is ‘it is in no way possible’ (ἔστι is accented on its first syllable because it means ‘it is possible’). μεθιέμεναι is the epic infinitive of μεθίημι ‘slacken’ with πολέμοιο, the genitive ‘from war’, as at 97.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἀκεώμεθα θᾶσσον·
sentences.tr: all’ akeōmetha thasson·
sentences.l: But let us heal, more quickly;
sentences.i: But let us mend things, and quickly;
sentences.n: He turns to the remedy. ἀκεώμεθα is the present subjunctive middle of ἀκέομαι ‘heal’, in the uncontracted epic form, used as an exhortation, ‘let us heal’; the object, the harm done by their slackness, is left to be understood. θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς, ‘more quickly’, here ‘the sooner the better’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀκεσταί τοι φρένες ἐσθλῶν.
sentences.tr: akestai toi phrenes esthlōn.
sentences.l: Healable, you know, are the wits of good men.
sentences.i: The wits of good men can be mended.
sentences.n: The ground for hope. ἀκεσταί is the verbal adjective of ἀκέομαι, ‘able to be healed’, feminine plural to agree with φρένες ‘wits’ (the table’s word), and it picks up ἀκεώμεθα. τοι is ‘you know’, a particle of appeal. ἐσθλῶν ‘of good men’ is a genitive of possession; as the table says of ἐσθλός at 2.365, in a battle context ‘good’ means brave.

sentences.t:
ὑμεῖς δ’ οὐκ ἔτι καλὰ μεθίετε θούριδος ἀλκῆς
πάντες ἄριστοι ἐόντες ἀνὰ στρατόν.
sentences.tr:
hymeis d’ ouk eti kala methiete thouridos alkēs
pantes aristoi eontes ana straton.
sentences.l:
But you, no longer finely, slacken from impetuous might,
all of you the best being throughout the army.
sentences.i: But it is no longer a fine thing, this slackening of yours from impetuous might, when you are all the best men in the army.
sentences.n: The rebuke proper. ὑμεῖς δέ ‘but you’ opens the contrast with the cowards of the next lines. καλά is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘finely’; οὐκ ἔτι καλά, ‘no longer finely’, says that the way they slacken is not a good thing, and the English turns the adverb into a comment on the slackening. μεθίετε is the present of μεθίημι ‘slacken’, with the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς, the table’s ‘impetuous might’ (4.234). πάντες ἄριστοι ἐόντες is ‘all being the best’ (ἐόντες the Ionic participle of εἰμί, ‘being’), and ἀνὰ στρατόν ‘throughout the army’. The unit ends at a full stop that falls inside the line.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν ἔγωγε
ἀνδρὶ μαχεσσαίμην ὅς τις πολέμοιο μεθείη
λυγρὸς ἐών·
sentences.tr:
oud’ an egōge
andri machessaimēn hos tis polemoio metheiē
lygros eōn·
sentences.i: Nor would I, for my part, fight with a man who slackened from war, a sorry creature as he is;
sentences.n: He would not be hard on a born coward. οὐδ’ ἂν … μαχεσσαίμην is the optative with ἄν, ‘I would not fight’; μαχεσσαίμην is the epic aorist of μάχομαι (with the doubled σ), and takes the dative ἀνδρί ‘with a man’. The ‘fight’ is a quarrel or a rebuke, not a battle. ὅς τις … μεθείη is a general relative clause with the optative (‘any man who should slacken’), μεθείη being the aorist optative of μεθίημι with the genitive πολέμοιο. λυγρός is the table’s ‘grievous’, said here of a man, as in the Odyssey’s ‘grievous as you are’ to a beggar; the English says ‘a sorry creature’, the man whose nature is poor. ἐών is the Ionic participle ‘being’.

sentences.t: ὑμῖν δὲ νεμεσσῶμαι περὶ κῆρι.
sentences.tr: hymin de nemessōmai peri kēri.
sentences.l: but at you I feel resentment, exceedingly, in my heart.
sentences.i: but I feel resentment at you, deep in my heart.
sentences.n: The contrast: with these men, because they are good, he is angry. νεμεσσῶμαι is the contracted present middle of νεμεσσάω ‘feel resentment’ (the table’s word) and takes the dative ὑμῖν ‘at you’. περί is here an adverb, ‘exceedingly’, and κῆρι is the dative of κῆρ ‘heart’ (a different word from κήρ ‘death-spirit’, which has a different accent).

sentences.t:
ὦ πέπονες τάχα δή τι κακὸν ποιήσετε μεῖζον
τῇδε μεθημοσύνῃ·
sentences.tr:
ō pepones tacha dē ti kakon poiēsete meizon
tēide methēmosynēi·
sentences.l:
O good ones, soon indeed some greater evil you will do
through this slackness;
sentences.i: My good fellows, soon you will do some greater evil through this slackness;
sentences.n: A prediction. ὦ πέπονες is the address that the table renders ‘good fellows’ at 2.235: the meaning of πέπων is not known, and the tone is read as scornful. τάχα δή is ‘soon indeed’; κακὸν … μεῖζον is ‘a greater evil’, and ποιήσετε is the future of ποιέω ‘do, make’. τῇδε μεθημοσύνῃ is the dative of cause, ‘through this slackness’ (μεθημοσύνη ‘slackness’, as at 108). The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐν φρεσὶ θέσθε ἕκαστος
αἰδῶ καὶ νέμεσιν·
sentences.tr:
all’ en phresi thesthe hekastos
aidō kai nemesin·
sentences.l:
but in your wits put, each man,
shame and resentment;
sentences.i: but each of you, put shame and resentment in your wits;
sentences.n: What he asks of them. θέσθε is the aorist middle imperative of τίθημι ‘put (in yourselves)’; ἐν φρεσί is ‘in the wits’ (the table’s word), and ἕκαστος ‘each man’ is singular, in apposition to the plural ‘you’. αἰδῶ is the accusative of αἰδώς ‘shame’, the sense of shame before one’s fellows, and νέμεσις is ‘resentment’, the table’s word: here it is the resentment that others will feel at a man who shames himself. The English keeps the two nouns.

sentences.t: δὴ γὰρ μέγα νεῖκος ὄρωρεν.
sentences.tr: dē gar mega neikos orōren.
sentences.l: for now a great quarrel has arisen.
sentences.i: for a great quarrel has now arisen.
sentences.n: His reason. δὴ γάρ is ‘for now’. ὄρωρεν is the perfect of ὄρνυμι in its intransitive sense, ‘has risen, has arisen’, a different use from the transitive ‘roused’ of ὦρσεν at 83. νεῖκος is ‘quarrel’, the table’s word, here the fighting itself, the quarrel being settled by arms.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δὴ παρὰ νηυσὶ βοὴν ἀγαθὸς πολεμίζει
καρτερός, ἔρρηξεν δὲ πύλας καὶ μακρὸν ὀχῆα.
sentences.tr:
Hektōr dē para nēusi boēn agathos polemizei
karteros, errēxen de pylas kai makron ochēa.
sentences.l:
Hector indeed by the ships, good at the war-cry, is fighting,
strong, and he has broken the gates and the long bar.”
sentences.i: Hector, good at the war-cry, is fighting at the ships, strong as he is, and he has broken the gates and the long bar.”
sentences.n: The cause of the alarm: Hector is at the ships, through the gate. βοὴν ἀγαθός is the table’s ‘good at the war-cry’, καρτερός is ‘strong’, and παρὰ νηυσί ‘at the ships’. ἔρρηξεν is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, and English puts it as a perfect, ‘has broken’. πύλας ‘gates’ and μακρὸν ὀχῆα ‘the long bar’ (the table’s ὀχεύς, 12.121) are the gates and bar of the Achaean wall, which Hector broke at the end of the previous book. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὥς ῥα κελευτιόων γαιήοχος ὦρσεν Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr: hōs rha keleutioōn gaiēochos ōrsen Achaious.
sentences.l: So then, giving orders, the earth-holder roused the Achaeans.
sentences.i: So the earth-holder, calling out his orders, roused the Achaeans.
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins here. This line closes the scene opened at 83, repeating γαιήοχος ὦρσεν Ἀχαιούς ‘the earth-holder roused the Achaeans’, still without a name. ὥς ῥα is ‘so, then’. κελευτιόων, a rare verb built on κελεύω ‘bid’, is the participle ‘giving orders’ (here, the speech just heard).

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ Αἴαντας δοιοὺς ἵσταντο φάλαγγες
καρτεραί,
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ar’ Aiantas doious histanto phalanges
karterai,
sentences.l:
And around the two Ajaxes took their stand the battle-lines,
strong ones,
sentences.i: And around the two Ajaxes the strong battle-lines took their stand,
sentences.n: Poseidon’s work shows in the ranks that form round the two Ajaxes. ἀμφί governs Αἴαντας δοιούς, the plural of the name with δοιός ‘two’, ‘the two Ajaxes’, as the table renders the pair. ἵσταντο is the imperfect middle of ἵστημι, ‘took their stand’; φάλαγγες ‘battle-lines’ is the subject, and καρτεραί ‘strong’ agrees with it. The unit ends at the comma before the relative clause.

sentences.t:
ἃς οὔτ’ ἄν κεν Ἄρης ὀνόσαιτο μετελθὼν
οὔτε κ’ Ἀθηναίη λαοσσόος·
sentences.tr:
has out’ an ken Arēs onosaito metelthōn
oute k’ Athēnaiē laossoos·
sentences.l:
which neither Ares would find fault with, coming among them,
nor Athena, rouser of the people;
sentences.i: lines that not even Ares would find fault with if he came among them, nor Athena, rouser of the people;
sentences.n: A compliment to the lines: not even the gods of war could fault them. ἃς is the relative, ‘which’, referring to the φάλαγγες. ἄν and κεν together mark the optative ὀνόσαιτο ‘would find fault with’ (ὄνομαι); μετελθών ‘coming among them’, an aorist participle, carries the sense of ‘if he came’. Ἄρης is the god. οὔτε κ’ Ἀθηναίη takes the same verb (κ’ is κε elided). λαοσσόος, ‘people-rousing’ in l and ‘rouser of the people’ in the English, follows the Odyssey table’s λαοσσόος, there said of Amphiaraus; its derivation is disputed, and ‘saving the people’ is also an ancient reading.

sentences.t:
οἳ γὰρ ἄριστοι
κρινθέντες Τρῶάς τε καὶ Ἕκτορα δῖον ἔμιμνον,
φράξαντες δόρυ δουρί, σάκος σάκεϊ προθελύμνῳ·
sentences.tr:
hoi gar aristoi
krinthentes Trōas te kai Hektora dion emimnon,
phraxantes dory douri, sakos sakeï prothelymnōi·
sentences.i: for these, the best men, picked out for the place, stood up to the Trojans and heavenly Hector, locking spear with spear and shield with shield, layer on layer;
sentences.n: Why the lines were so good: they were the picked best. οἳ is ‘they’ (the pointing article, here ‘these’), γάρ gives the reason, and ἄριστοι is ‘the best’, with κρινθέντες the aorist passive participle of κρίνω ‘separate, pick out’. ἔμιμνον is the imperfect of μίμνω = μένω, ‘awaited, stood up to’ (as at 106), taking the accusatives Τρῶας and Ἕκτορα δῖον, ‘heavenly Hector’ (δῖος, the table’s word). φράξαντες is the aorist participle of φράσσω ‘fence, close up’, with the accusatives δόρυ and σάκος and the datives δουρί and σάκεϊ, ‘spear with spear, shield with shield’. προθελύμνῳ is a word whose meaning is not known for certain: it seems to contain θέλυμνα ‘the base, the roots’ (the table has προθέλυμνα ‘torn up from the base’ at 9.541), and ‘in layers’ is a guess, which the English follows with ‘layer on layer’.

sentences.t: ἀσπὶς ἄρ’ ἀσπίδ’ ἔρειδε, κόρυς κόρυν, ἀνέρα δ’ ἀνήρ·
sentences.tr: aspis ar’ aspid’ ereide, korys koryn, anera d’ anēr·
sentences.l: shield pressed on shield, helmet on helmet, and man on man;
sentences.i: shield pressed on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man;
sentences.n: The packing of the line. ἀσπίς, κόρυς and ἀνήρ are each the subject of ἔρειδε, the imperfect of ἐρείδω ‘press, lean’, with its own accusative (ἀσπίδ’, κόρυν, ἀνέρα) after it, so each thing leans on its like. ἀσπίς ‘shield’ and κόρυς ‘helmet’ are the ordinary words.

sentences.t:
ψαῦον δ’ ἱππόκομοι κόρυθες λαμπροῖσι φάλοισι
νευόντων, ὡς πυκνοὶ ἐφέστασαν ἀλλήλοισιν·
sentences.tr:
psauon d’ hippokomoi korythes lamproisi phaloisi
neuontōn, hōs pyknoi ephestasan allēloisin·
sentences.l:
and the horse-plumed helmets touched with their bright ridges
as the men nodded, so close they were standing to one another;
sentences.i: and the helmets with horsehair plumes touched one another with their bright ridges as the men nodded, so closely did they stand to one another;
sentences.n: Helmet touching helmet. ψαῦον is the imperfect of ψαύω ‘touch’, with no object stated, since the helmets touch one another. ἱππόκομοι κόρυθες is ‘horse-plumed helmets’ (ἱπποκόμος, 12.339), and φάλοισι is the dative of φάλος, taken to be the ridge of the helmet that carries the plume (the sense is not certain, as at 3.362). νευόντων is the genitive plural of the participle of νεύω ‘nod’, with an unspoken ‘of the men’: ‘as they nodded’. ὡς πυκνοὶ ἐφέστασαν ἀλλήλοισιν is ‘how closely they stood against one another’ (ἐφέστασαν an epic past of ἐφίστημι ‘stand near’).

sentences.t:
ἔγχεα δ’ ἐπτύσσοντο θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν
σειόμεν’·
sentences.tr:
enchea d’ eptyssonto thraseiaōn apo cheirōn
seiomen’·
sentences.l:
and the spears were bending, from bold hands
being shaken;
sentences.i: and the spears bent as they were shaken in bold hands;
sentences.n: ἔγχεα ‘spears’ is the subject of ἐπτύσσοντο, the imperfect of πτύσσω ‘fold’, in the middle: ‘were folding, were bending’. The sense, shafts flexing as they are shaken, is a guess from the verb, and the English says ‘bent’. θρασειάων is the epic genitive plural feminine of θρασύς ‘bold’, with χειρῶν ‘hands’, and σειόμεν’ is the elided participle σειόμενα ‘being shaken’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἰθὺς φρόνεον, μέμασαν δὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ithys phroneon, memasan de machesthai.
sentences.l: and they were minded straight on, and were eager to fight.
sentences.i: and their minds were set straight ahead, and they were eager to fight.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the men of the lines, contrasted with their spears. ἰθύς ‘straight on’ is the adverb, as at 12.453, and φρόνεον is the imperfect of φρονέω ‘think, have in mind’: their purpose was single and straight ahead. μέμασαν is a past form of μέμαα ‘I am eager’ (the table’s ‘eager’), and μάχεσθαι is ‘to fight’.

sentences.t: Τρῶες δὲ προὔτυψαν ἀολλέες,
sentences.tr: Trōes de proutypsan aollees,
sentences.l: And the Trojans pushed forward, in a close mass,
sentences.i: And the Trojans pushed forward in a close mass,
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins here: the attack. προὔτυψαν is an aorist of προτύπτω, ‘pushed forward’. ἀολλέες is ‘in a close mass’ (the table, 5.498). The unit ends at the comma, and Hector is named next.

sentences.t:
ἦρχε δ’ ἄρ’ Ἕκτωρ
ἀντικρὺ μεμαώς,
sentences.tr:
ērche d’ ar’ Hektōr
antikry memaōs,
sentences.l:
and led them Hector,
straight on, eager,
sentences.i: and Hector led them, eager, head-on,
sentences.n: ἦρχε is the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead’, here without an object, ‘led (them)’; δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and so’. ἀντικρύ is ‘head-on’ (the table’s word for fighting), and μεμαώς is the masculine perfect participle of μέμαα, ‘eager’, agreeing with Ἕκτωρ. The unit ends at the comma before the simile.

sentences.t:
ὀλοοίτροχος ὣς ἀπὸ πέτρης,
ὅν τε κατὰ στεφάνης ποταμὸς χειμάρροος ὤσῃ
ῥήξας ἀσπέτῳ ὄμβρῳ ἀναιδέος ἔχματα πέτρης·
sentences.tr:
olooitrochos hōs apo petrēs,
hon te kata stephanēs potamos cheimarroos ōsēi
rhēxas aspetōi ombrōi anaideos echmata petrēs·
sentences.i: like a rolling boulder from a rock, which a winter torrent pushes down from the brow after breaking, with boundless rain, the supports of the ruthless rock;
sentences.n: The simile of the boulder. ὀλοοίτροχος names a stone that rolls or runs: -τροχος is from the root of τρέχω ‘run’ and τροχός ‘wheel’. The first half of the word is disputed (ὀλοός ‘ruinous’ is one guess), so the English says only ‘rolling boulder’; ὣς here stands after the noun, ‘like’. ὅν τε … ὤσῃ is a relative clause with τε of general truth: ὤσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ὠθέω ‘push’, and ὅν (the boulder) is its object; κατὰ στεφάνης is ‘down from the brow’ (στεφάνη ‘rim, crown’, here the edge of a height). ποταμὸς χειμάρροος is ‘a winter-flowing river’, a torrent (χεῖμα ‘winter’ + ῥέω ‘flow’). ῥήξας is ‘having broken’, ἀσπέτῳ ὄμβρῳ ‘with boundless rain’ (ἄσπετος, the table’s ‘boundless’), and ἔχματα (from ἔχω ‘hold’) the things that hold something in place, ‘supports’. ἀναιδέος, ‘shameless’ in l, is said of a rock that does not give way, with no feeling: ‘ruthless’ in the English, the table’s word for a stone (4.521).

sentences.t:
ὕψι δ’ ἀναθρῴσκων πέτεται, κτυπέει δέ θ’ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ
ὕλη·
sentences.tr:
hypsi d’ anathrōiskōn petetai, ktypeei de th’ hyp’ autou
hylē·
sentences.l:
and high, leaping up, it flies, and thunders beneath it
the forest;
sentences.i: and leaping up it flies high, and the forest thunders beneath it;
sentences.n: The boulder’s course. ὕψι ‘high’ and ἀναθρῴσκων ‘leaping up’; πέτεται is the present of πέτομαι ‘fly’, said of the boulder. κτυπέει is the uncontracted present of κτυπέω ‘thunder’, the table’s word, and θ’ is τε of general truth. ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ‘beneath it’ is the genitive after ὑπό, and ὕλη ‘forest’ is the subject. The unit ends at the ano teleia, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀσφαλέως θέει ἔμπεδον, εἷος ἵκηται
ἰσόπεδον,
sentences.tr:
ho d’ asphaleōs theei empedon, heios hikētai
isopedon,
sentences.l:
and it runs securely, steadily, until it comes
to level ground,
sentences.i: and it runs on surely and steadily until it reaches level ground,
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and it’ (the boulder) is the article as a pronoun. ἀσφαλέως ‘securely’ and ἔμπεδον ‘steadily’ are adverbs; θέει is the uncontracted present of θέω ‘run’. εἷος is the epic ‘until’ (Attic ἕως), with ἵκηται, the aorist subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to’, again in a general statement. ἰσόπεδον is ‘level’ (ἴσος ‘equal’ + πέδον ‘ground’), here a neuter accusative, ‘to level ground’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: τότε δ’ οὔ τι κυλίνδεται ἐσσύμενός περ·
sentences.tr: tote d’ ou ti kylindetai essymenos per·
sentences.l: then it does not at all roll, hurrying though it is;
sentences.i: then it does not roll at all, hurrying though it is;
sentences.n: τότε ‘then’ answers εἷος. οὔ τι is ‘not at all’; κυλίνδεται is the present middle of κυλίνδω ‘roll’. ἐσσύμενος is the participle of σεύομαι ‘hurry’ (the table’s ‘hurrying’), and περ means ‘though’. The unit ends at the ano teleia, the last clause of the simile.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἕκτωρ εἷος μὲν ἀπείλει μέχρι θαλάσσης
ῥέα διελεύσεσθαι κλισίας καὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
κτείνων·
sentences.tr:
hōs Hektōr heios men apeilei mechri thalassēs
rhea dieleusesthai klisias kai nēas Achaiōn
kteinōn·
sentences.i: So Hector, for a time, threatened that he would easily make his way through the huts and ships of the Achaeans as far as the sea, killing as he went;
sentences.n: The simile is applied: Hector is the boulder, unchecked until the level ground. ὣς Ἕκτωρ is ‘so Hector’. εἷος μέν is ‘for a time, so long as’, and is answered by ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ‘but when’ in the next unit. ἀπείλει is the imperfect of ἀπειλέω ‘threaten’ (the table’s word), and it takes the future infinitive διελεύσεσθαι ‘that he would go through’ (διέρχομαι), with κλισίας καὶ νῆας ‘the huts and the ships’ as its objects. ῥέα is the epic ῥεῖα ‘easily’ (see 90), μέχρι θαλάσσης ‘as far as the sea’, and κτείνων ‘killing’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πυκινῇς ἐνέκυρσε φάλαγξι
στῆ ῥα μάλ’ ἐγχριμφθείς·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē pykinēis enekyrse phalanxi
stē rha mal’ enchrimphtheis·
sentences.l:
but when indeed he met with the close-packed battle-lines,
he stood, quite pressed up close;
sentences.i: but when he ran into the close-packed battle-lines, he stopped, pressed hard up against them;
sentences.n: The check. ἐνέκυρσε is the aorist of ἐγκυρέω ‘meet with, chance upon’, taking the dative φάλαγξι (the epic dative plural of φάλαγξ, ‘battle-line’), with πυκινῇς (epic -ῃς for -αις) ‘close-packed’. στῆ ῥα is ‘then he stood still’, from the aorist of ἵστημι. ἐγχριμφθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἐγχρίμπτω ‘press close against’: he was pressed up against the line, and brought to a stop; μάλα is ‘quite’. The unit ends at the ano teleia, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀντίοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
νύσσοντες ξίφεσίν τε καὶ ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισιν
ὦσαν ἀπὸ σφείων·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ antioi huies Achaiōn
nyssontes xiphesin te kai enchesin amphigyoisin
ōsan apo spheiōn·
sentences.i: and the sons of the Achaeans, facing him, stabbed at him with swords and double-pointed spears and pushed him away from themselves;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the Achaeans of the line, with υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘the sons of the Achaeans’ (the table, 1.162) in apposition, and ἀντίοι ‘facing’ in the nominative plural. νύσσοντες is the participle of νύσσω ‘stab, thrust’; ξίφεσιν and ἔγχεσιν are datives of the means, ‘with swords’ and ‘with spears’. ἀμφιγύοισιν is ‘double-pointed’, the Odyssey’s rendering of a word of uncertain meaning. ὦσαν is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’, with the object (Hector) unspoken, and σφείων is the epic form of σφῶν ‘of themselves’, so ‘away from themselves’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ χασσάμενος πελεμίχθη.
sentences.tr: ho de chassamenos pelemichthē.
sentences.l: and he, having given ground, was shaken.
sentences.i: and he gave ground, reeling.
sentences.n: Hector is the one pushed back. ὃ δέ ‘and he’; χασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of χάζομαι ‘give ground, draw back’, and πελεμίχθη the aorist passive of πελεμίζω ‘shake’, ‘was shaken’; the English joins the two, ‘gave ground, reeling’.

sentences.t: ἤϋσεν δὲ διαπρύσιον Τρώεσσι γεγωνώς·
sentences.tr: ēÿsen de diaprysion Trōessi gegōnōs·
sentences.l: And he shouted piercingly, calling aloud to the Trojans:
sentences.i: And he shouted piercingly, calling aloud to the Trojans:
sentences.n: The speech introduction for Hector’s call. ἤϋσεν is the aorist of ἀΰω ‘shout’ (the edition prints the diaeresis), and διαπρύσιον ‘piercingly’ is a neuter used as an adverb. γεγωνώς is the perfect participle of γέγωνα, which has the sense of a present, ‘calling aloud’, here ‘so as to be heard far off’; Τρώεσσι is the epic dative plural, ‘to the Trojans’.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες καὶ Λύκιοι καὶ Δάρδανοι ἀγχιμαχηταὶ
παρμένετ’·
sentences.tr:
Trōes kai Lykioi kai Dardanoi anchimachētai
parmenet’·
sentences.l:
“Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, close-fighters,
stand by;
sentences.i: “Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, fighters at close quarters, stand by;
sentences.n: Hector calls on the Trojans and their allies. The address Τρῶες καὶ Λύκιοι καὶ Δάρδανοι is stock, as is ἀγχιμαχηταί ‘fighters at close quarters’ (the table’s ἀγχιμαχητής). παρμένετ’ is παραμένετε, the imperative of παραμένω ‘stay beside, hold out’, with no object stated: ‘stand by’, hold the line. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὔ τοι δηρὸν ἐμὲ σχήσουσιν Ἀχαιοὶ
καὶ μάλα πυργηδὸν σφέας αὐτοὺς ἀρτύναντες,
sentences.tr:
ou toi dēron eme schēsousin Achaioi
kai mala pyrgēdon spheas autous artynantes,
sentences.l:
not for long, you know, will they hold me back, the Achaeans,
even very much, tower-fashion, themselves having drawn up,
sentences.i: the Achaeans will not hold me back for long, however much they have drawn themselves up like a tower,
sentences.n: οὔ τοι δηρόν is ‘not for long, you may be sure’ (τοι an appeal, δηρόν ‘for a long time’). σχήσουσιν is the future of ἔχω ‘hold back’, with ἐμέ ‘me’ as its object. καὶ μάλα is ‘even very much so’ and makes the participle concessive: ‘however much they have drawn themselves up’. πυργηδόν is an adverb, ‘tower-fashion’, σφέας αὐτούς ‘themselves’, and ἀρτύναντες the aorist participle of ἀρτύνω ‘arrange, draw up’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὀΐω χάσσονται ὑπ’ ἔγχεος, εἰ ἐτεόν με
ὦρσε θεῶν ὤριστος, ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης.
sentences.tr:
all’ oïō chassontai hyp’ encheos, ei eteon me
ōrse theōn ōristos, erigdoupos posis Hērēs.
sentences.l:
but I think they will give ground before the spear, if truly me
roused the best of the gods, the loud-crashing husband of Hera.”
sentences.i: but I think they will give ground before my spear, if it is truly the best of the gods who has roused me, the loud-crashing husband of Hera.”
sentences.n: Hector ends by claiming Zeus’s backing. ὀΐω is ‘I think’ (the epic form of οἴομαι); χάσσονται is the future of χάζομαι ‘give ground’ (compare χασσάμενος at 148); ὑπ’ ἔγχεος is ‘before the spear’, with ὑπό and the genitive of cause. εἰ ἐτεόν is ‘if truly’, ἐτεόν being the neuter as an adverb; ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι (see 83), with με as its object. ὤριστος is ὁ ἄριστος, the article fused with ἄριστος, ‘the best’. The god is Zeus, who is not named: ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης ‘loud-crashing husband of Hera’ is his stock title, translated every time. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn otryne menos kai thymon hekastou.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins here. ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’, the stock close to a speech. ὄτρυνε is the aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, with the two objects μένος ‘might’ and θυμόν ‘heart’ and the one genitive ἑκάστου ‘of each man’ for both.

sentences.t:
Δηΐφοβος δ’ ἐν τοῖσι μέγα φρονέων ἐβεβήκει
Πριαμίδης,
sentences.tr:
Dēïphobos d’ en toisi mega phroneōn ebebēkei
Priamidēs,
sentences.l:
And Deiphobus among them, greatly thinking, had gone,
Priam’s-son,
sentences.i: And Deiphobus, son of Priam, went forward among them, full of proud thoughts,
sentences.n: Deiphobus, named once before among the Trojan leaders (12.94), now has a part of his own; he is a son of Priam, and not Hector. Δηΐφοβος has the diaeresis as printed. ἐν τοῖσι ‘among them’ is the article as a pronoun, the Trojans. μέγα φρονέων is the table’s ‘full of proud thoughts’ (11.296); ἐβεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone’, with the force of ‘was on his way’. Πριαμίδης is the patronymic ‘son of Priam’, held back to the start of the next line. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
πρόσθεν δ’ ἔχεν ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην
κοῦφα ποσὶ προβιβὰς καὶ ὑπασπίδια προποδίζων.
sentences.tr:
prosthen d’ echen aspida pantos’ eïsēn
koupha posi probibas kai hypaspidia propodizōn.
sentences.l:
and in front he held his shield, equal on every side,
lightly with his feet striding forward, and under the shield stepping forward.
sentences.i: and held his shield, equal on every side, in front of him, striding forward lightly on his feet and advancing, step by step, under its cover.
sentences.n: He advances behind his shield. ἔχεν is the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω ‘held’, and πρόσθεν ‘in front’. ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην is the table’s ‘a shield equal on every side’, that is, a round one. κοῦφα is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘lightly’, with ποσί ‘on the feet’; προβιβάς is the participle of προβιβάω ‘stride forward’, and προποδίζων ‘stepping forward’ is built on πρό and πούς ‘foot’. ὑπασπίδια is an adverb, ‘under the shield’ (ὑπό + ἀσπίς), so he goes forward under cover.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δ’ αὐτοῖο τιτύσκετο δουρὶ φαεινῷ
καὶ βάλεν, οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτε, κατ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην
ταυρείην·
sentences.tr:
Mērionēs d’ autoio titysketo douri phaeinōi
kai balen, oud’ aphamarte, kat’ aspida pantos’ eïsēn
taureiēn·
sentences.i: Meriones took aim at him with his shining spear, and hit, and did not miss, the shield that was equal on every side, the one of bull’s hide;
sentences.n: Meriones answers with a throw. αὐτοῖο is the epic genitive of αὐτός ‘him’, the target, and τιτύσκετο is the imperfect middle of τιτύσκομαι ‘aim at’; δουρί is the epic dative of δόρυ ‘spear’, φαεινῷ ‘shining’. βάλεν is the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω ‘hit’, and οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτε is ‘and did not miss’ (ἀφαμαρτάνω); κατ’ ἀσπίδα governs the shield. ταυρείην is the adjective from ταῦρος ‘bull’, ‘of a bull’s hide’, agreeing with ἀσπίδα and held back to the start of the next line. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τῆς δ’ οὔ τι διήλασεν, ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρὶν
ἐν καυλῷ ἐάγη δολιχὸν δόρυ·
sentences.tr:
tēs d’ ou ti diēlasen, alla poly prin
en kaulōi eagē dolichon dory·
sentences.l:
but through it he did not drive at all, but long before
in the shaft was broken the long spear;
sentences.i: but he did not drive through it at all, for the long spear broke in the shaft well before that;
sentences.n: The spear fails. τῆς ‘of it’ is the shield (the article as a pronoun) in the genitive after διήλασεν ‘drove through’; οὔ τι is ‘not at all’; the Greek does not name the subject, Meriones or his spear, and the English has ‘he’. πολὺ πρίν is ‘long before’, before the point got through. ἐάγη is the aorist passive of ἄγνυμι ‘break’, here ‘was broken’; ἐν καυλῷ is ‘in the shaft’ (καυλός is the stem of a spear), and δολιχὸν δόρυ is the table’s ‘long spear’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 162.

sentences.t:
Δηΐφοβος δὲ
ἀσπίδα ταυρείην σχέθ’ ἀπὸ ἕο, δεῖσε δὲ θυμῷ
ἔγχος Μηριόναο δαΐφρονος·
sentences.tr:
Dēïphobos de
aspida taureiēn scheth’ apo heo, deise de thymōi
enchos Mērionao daïphronos·
sentences.i: and Deiphobus held his shield of bull’s hide away from himself, and feared in his heart the spear of wise-hearted Meriones;
sentences.n: Deiphobus’ side of it. σχέθ’ is the epic aorist of ἔχω, ‘held’; ἀπὸ ἕο is ‘away from himself’, ἕο being the epic genitive of the reflexive pronoun. δεῖσε is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’ and takes the accusative ἔγχος ‘spear’. Μηριόναο is the epic genitive of Μηριόνης, and δαΐφρονος is the house epithet, ‘wise-minded’ in l and ‘wise-hearted’ in the English: whether it means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed. The unit begins in the middle of 162, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως
ἂψ ἑτάρων εἰς ἔθνος ἐχάζετο,
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ hērōs
aps hetarōn eis ethnos echazeto,
sentences.l:
but he, the hero,
back to the company of his companions he drew away,
sentences.i: but the hero drew back to the company of his companions,
sentences.n: Meriones retreats. αὐτάρ ‘but’, and ὅ γε ‘he’ (Meriones, with γε emphatic); ἥρως is the plain title ‘hero’. ἂψ is ‘back’, and ἔθνος ἑταίρων ‘company of companions’ is the table’s phrase (ἑτάρων is the epic form of ἑταίρων). ἐχάζετο is the imperfect of χάζομαι ‘draw back’ (see 148).

sentences.t:
χώσατο δ’ αἰνῶς
ἀμφότερον, νίκης τε καὶ ἔγχεος ὃ ξυνέαξε.
sentences.tr:
chōsato d’ ainōs
amphoteron, nikēs te kai encheos ho xyneaxe.
sentences.l:
and he was angry, dreadfully,
on both counts, over the victory and over the spear which was broken up.
sentences.i: and he was dreadfully angry on both counts, over the victory and over the spear that had been shattered.
sentences.n: His anger. χώσατο is the aorist of χώομαι ‘be angry’, and αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’ is the table’s word. ἀμφότερον is ‘on both counts’, a neuter accusative of respect, spelled out by νίκης τε καὶ ἔγχεος, genitives of cause, ‘over the victory (that he missed) and over the spear’. ὅ is the neuter relative with ἔγχεος as its antecedent, and ξυνέαξε is the aorist active of συνάγνυμι ‘break to pieces’ (ξυν- is the old spelling of συν-); ὅ is its object, since this aorist is transitive (the spear’s own breaking was said with ἐάγη at 162); the Greek does not say who or what shattered it, and ‘was broken up’ in l and ‘had been shattered’ in the English leave that open.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι παρά τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
οἰσόμενος δόρυ μακρόν, ὅ οἱ κλισίηφι λέλειπτο.
sentences.tr:
bē d’ ienai para te klisias kai nēas Achaiōn
oisomenos dory makron, ho hoi klisiēphi leleipto.
sentences.l:
He went on his way, along the huts and the ships of the Achaeans,
to fetch a long spear, which for him in his hut had been left.
sentences.i: He set off along the huts and the ships of the Achaeans to fetch a long spear that had been left for him in his hut.
sentences.n: Meriones goes for another spear. βῆ δ’ ἰέναι, ‘he went on his way’, is a stock phrase for setting out (βῆ the aorist of βαίνω, ἰέναι the infinitive of εἶμι), and παρά τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας is ‘along the huts and the ships’, παρά with the accusative of the line passed. οἰσόμενος is the future middle participle of φέρω, ‘to fetch’ (a future participle of purpose); δόρυ μακρόν is ‘a long spear’. ὅ is the relative, οἱ is ‘for him’, κλισίηφι is ‘in the hut’ (the old ending -φι standing for a dative of place), and λέλειπτο is the pluperfect passive of λείπω, ‘had been left’. The part ends with him on his way.
